title: Day 46 · Week 6, Day 4 — Adventure: going up — altitude in the first trimester, the five studies that exist, the sleeping-altitude rule, and the one pill she shouldn't take
summary: The third Adventure episode: the ski week, the mountain town, the high city. Your baby is 5–7 mm at Carnegie stage 14, lens pits closing into vesicles — and already living at 'altitude': placental oxygen under 20 mmHg at 8 weeks, by design (Jauniaux 2000; Rodesch 1992; Eastman's 'Mount Everest in utero', 1954). The entire literature on pregnant altitude visitors is five small third-trimester studies and one survey (McManis 2021): a cable car to 2,228 m (transcutaneous PO2 71 → 58 mmHg, fetal heart rate 138 → 142, one smoker's fetus briefly slow), a chamber, ten commercial flights, seven women exercising to maximum at 6,000 ft (fetal heart rate unchanged; Artal 1995), and one Sherpa guide at 5,300 m — reassuring, and not one first-trimester woman among them. The resident data that people will quote: birthweight −102 g per 1,000 m in 3,836 Colorado births (Jensen & Moore 1997), pre-eclampsia 16% vs 3% at 3,100 m (Palmer 1999), growth restriction 16.8% vs 5.9% at 3,600 m in Bolivia (Keyes 2003) — nine months of placental work after 20 weeks, which is where every guideline draws its hard line. The real hazard is acute mountain sickness: 25% of 3,158 Colorado visitors, 65% within 12 hours, 3.5× for sea-level residents (Honigman 1993; CDC Yellow Book), with symptoms identical to Week 6 — so her PUQE score from Day 41 is the baseline. Acetazolamide: contraindicated in the first trimester by the UIAA on animal data; 50 human first-trimester exposures without a signal (Falardeau 2013) — reassuring, thin, and not for a holiday. The ascent profile from the Yellow Book (no first night above 2,750 m from low ground; 2–3 nights at 2,450–2,750; ≤500 m/day above 3,000; easy for 48 h) and the ceilings that agree: 2,500 m for short stays (UIAA; Huch 1996), 1,800–2,500 m for acclimatised moderate exercise (ACOG CO 804; Mottola 2018), 'prudent' not to sleep above 3,050 m (CDC). Falls, dry air, and the one risk Week 6 adds: distance to a transvaginal probe. Three worked trips and the bed-not-summit rule.
action: Tonight, ten minutes, with the next mountain trip open: write down the sleeping altitude for every night — the bed, not the lift-top. If any night is above 2,750 m and you arrive from low ground, add a night at 2,400–2,750 m on the way up; if any night is above 3,050 m, move it lower or move the trip, and make that the OB question this week. Find the nearest hospital with obstetric ultrasound to where you'll sleep, with the drive time, and save it in both phones under the Day 28 after-hours number. Put the Day 39 bottle and the PUQE score on the packing list. No acetazolamide this pregnancy — the ascent profile replaces it.
